note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 25-year-old woman (DOB 1 Oct 1999) with acute progressive upper lip swelling and respiratory symptoms beginning ~30 minutes after eating prawn soup.
- Clinician suspected anaphylactic reaction; ambulance/emergency services were called and patient advised to take available oral antihistamine and await ambulance; follow-up advised after hospital review.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute allergic reaction with suspected anaphylaxis
- Presentation: Acute onset lip swelling starting in left corner then involving upper lip, began ~30 minutes after eating prawn soup (evening, ~7:00 PM); swelling progressive and described as "getting bigger."
- Associated symptoms: Subjective difficulty breathing, sensation of throat closing, possible chest tightness, dizziness.
- Systems review: Respiratory difficulty and throat sensation positive; no documented rash, vomiting, or gastrointestinal symptoms mentioned.
- Examination findings: Visible swelling of upper lip reported by patient; no documented airway exam, lung auscultation, or vital signs in transcript.
- Relevant history: Prior episode ~1 year ago with morning facial swelling and breathing difficulty after eating (possibly curry) while intoxicated; childhood severe allergic reaction reported by mother requiring injection/hospital at ~age 6 (patient uncertain of details).
- Specialist/allied health: Emergency ambulance was contacted/arranged by clinician; patient instructed to call emergency services (999) if not already done and to await ambulance.
- Clinical impression/differential: Treating clinician suspected anaphylactic reaction.

Issue 2: Asthma (chronic)
- History: Patient reports known asthma.
- Medications: Uses salbutamol inhaler regularly (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Recent status: No objective respiratory exam or peak flow documented; patient used salbutamol historically during prior episode but no information on current use during this event.

Issue 3: Known peanut allergy and uncertain antihistamine use
- History: Lifelong peanut allergy reported.
- Prior management: Mother reported a severe allergic reaction in childhood requiring injection/hospital (patient uncertain).
- Current meds: Patient reports sometimes taking antihistamines but cannot specify which (antihistamine name/dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Current availability: At time of call, patient initially had no antihistamines on person; a family member subsequently present reported they do have antihistamines available.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Antihistamines (unspecified) — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Peanut allergy (patient-reported).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Recurrent allergic reactions: childhood severe reaction (mother-reported, age ~6), prior episode ~1 year ago with swelling and breathing difficulty.

Social History:
- Patient alone at time of initial call; another person (mother) arrived during consult.
- Alcohol: Patient reported being "quite drunk" during a prior allergic episode (~1 year ago). No current alcohol use frequency documented.
- Smoking status and living arrangements not documented.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care, screening, vaccinations, or recent optometry/skin checks documented in the consult.

Physical Examination:
- Vital signs: Not documented.
- Findings: Patient-reported progressive upper lip swelling; subjective dyspnea, chest tightness, dizziness. No clinician-performed exam details recorded.

Plan:
- Immediate: Ambulance/emergency services to be called and attend (clinician initiated call; patient/mother instructed to call 999 if not already done).
- Interim treatment: Take available oral antihistamine immediately while awaiting ambulance (patient advised to take what is available at home).
- Hospital care: Attend emergency department for assessment and treatment of suspected anaphylaxis (ambulance transport).
- Follow-up: Patient advised to contact the clinician/service after hospital visit for further management and possible provision/arrangement of "injections and things like that" (note: specifics not documented).

document_quality — Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: objective vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation), airway/respiratory exam findings, documented administration of any medications (antihistamine/epinephrine), exact antihistamine names and doses, details of prior hospitalizations or epinephrine use, allergy testing results, smoking status.
- Internal conflicts: Initial chart note referenced a "sandwich" as the trigger but patient clarified the trigger was prawn soup — conflict noted and clarified by patient. Patient uncertain about which antihistamines she uses and uncertain about details of childhood injection/hospitalization.
- Transcript quality: Generally intelligible; occasional emotional distress and short interruptions (patient dizziness) but clinically relevant information is clear.
